chunk_text:
Good evening. Today is the third last class for Module 3. On Tuesday, we talked a lot about neural networks and a bit on the math of how they work. Today, there won't be a lot of math; it's mostly applied, sharing more about the transition from traditional computer vision and how deep learning influences and adapts to make inferences on images. We'll also discuss improving some training. We are almost towards the end. Next Tuesday, for NLP, we'll go through the basics, and for the final class, we'll relate deep learning back to NLP.

Today, we'll focus on image inference. We'll use what we've seen in neural networks and introduce additional components to these building blocks. This allows us to take advantage of certain known properties of images to train models that are very good at predicting image data. Our goal is to discuss the motivation from an intuition perspective, then see how to apply Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in the notebook, and finally, introduce the idea of utilizing pre-trained models, or transfer learning, which forms the foundation for deep learning in applied contexts.

On Tuesday, we saw the basic building blocks from neural networks, specifically the feed-forward neural network, which uses linear layers with added nonlinear components to make the network more expressive. We even applied it to image data in the notebook. So, what has changed? We will add additional components to capture certain properties that we want the model to directly access. Neural networks are powerful for unstructured data because their LEGO blocks are customizable, allowing the resulting architecture to have an inductive bias that is good for specific unstructured data.

You can reshape and flatten your image data, as you saw in the notebook. From three dimensions, you can flatten it to two dimensions. For a feed-forward neural network, you flatten all of it into a single dimension. So, for your original data, you have `n` by height by width by channel (where `n` is the number of images). In the notebook, we flattened this into tabular data: `n` by (height * width * channel). I'll show the intuition why this is not ideal later. The neural network doesn't really know or care, but if you flatten it, you might not be making the best use of the image's properties. You'll see later why the convolutional neural network, created by Yann LeCun, performs very well for image data.

Keywords: convolutional neural networks, cnn, feed-forward neural network, image flattening, spatial information, inductive bias, image properties, deep learning for images, yann lecun

Questions this chunk answers:
- Why are CNNs better than feed-forward networks for image data?
- What is inductive bias in the context of CNNs?
- How does flattening an image affect a neural network?
- What are the benefits of CNNs for computer vision tasks?

chunk_text:
Computer vision is not just deep learning. When people think about computer vision, how you make inference on images and preprocess them has been around for quite some time. There have been traditional methods for image inference. It's not that image analysis or computer vision didn't exist before deep learning; it's just that with deep learning, instead of rule-based or manual methods, you can now build neural networks to predict things using image data.

At a basic level, you can formulate the problem as using image input for classification or regression. You still want to predict certain things. You can also go very deep into object detection, but that's not our main topic today. We're focusing solely on how to make inference, regression, or classification output from image data using a target label.

Computer vision has been around for a long time. Yann LeCun popularized and created the convolutional neural network block, which improved training on image data. While we've recently moved beyond CNNs for some problems, they still work for many. Deep learning has significantly evolved the extent to which we can train image data.

One very useful application is Optical Character Recognition (OCR). If you have an image with characters, you can convert them to text. The model predicts and outputs the text it recognizes from an image. OCR has many use cases, such as converting PDF documents to text-based formats or encoding real-world map information into data. Next week, we'll discuss NLP and how it translates to deep learning, including large language models.

Keywords: computer vision history, traditional computer vision, deep learning computer vision, ocr, optical character recognition, image to text, yann lecun cnn

Questions this chunk answers:
- What is OCR and how is it used?
- Did computer vision exist before deep learning?
- Who created the convolutional neural network?
- What are some basic applications of computer vision?

chunk_text:
Many tools involve computer vision. For example, home security cameras often have features to detect if a person is human or if there's a package. This all uses computer vision.

We won't go very deep into object detection today. Our focus is on predicting classification or continuous values from image input. However, for other computer vision applications, you can do object detection. The concepts we cover today are still relevant, but the architecture will differ slightly. For object detection, you usually want pixel-level prediction, including bounding boxes to locate the object and classification to identify what it is.

One famous model for this is YOLO (You Only Look Once), which allows for multiple classes. There are even newer models that predict an unlimited number of classes. Object detection has many applications: medical imaging (detecting areas in CT scans), autonomous vehicles (detecting pedestrians, cars, traffic signs), retail (tracking products), and surveillance (spotting intruders).

Keywords: object detection, yolo, bounding box, pixel-level prediction, computer vision applications, autonomous vehicles, medical imaging, surveillance

Questions this chunk answers:
- What is object detection in computer vision?
- How does YOLO work for object detection?
- What are practical applications of object detection?
- What kind of output does an object detection model provide?

topic: What you see VS what the computer sees
chunk_text:
It's important to understand that deep learning algorithms do not process data the way humans do. I mentioned this briefly: under the hood, the model doesn't truly "know." We use quantitative metrics to direct the model, passing gradients from the loss all the way back to each building block during backpropagation. From an image perspective, the model doesn't have a concept of how humans think.

What was brilliant about CNNs is that when humans created the algorithm, they incorporated thoughts that try to mimic how humans perceive. These inventions are very useful. On Tuesday, you saw how neural networks interact, even though mathematically it's just dot products. The famous illustration of neurons interacting emulates how our biological neurons work: individually, they might not do much, but together, they can make inferences.

Similarly for images, you'll become familiar with the idea that they are ultimately just data. An image is essentially a three-dimensional matrix: height, width, and channel. When working with computer vision, you need to be comfortable with n-dimensional matrices. An image has height, width, and typically three color channels. The model perceives this as a matrix, and we manipulate and project these to other dimensions. The computer sees a matrix.

Similarly, when you talk to a large language model, it doesn't truly "know" what you're saying. It processes encoded text as tokens, which are encoded with certain information, and its goal is to make predictions. It doesn't see what you think it's seeing; it's just processing these three RGB channels. If you didn't know images consist of three channels, now you do.

Keywords: computer vision perception, human vs computer vision, image as matrix, rgb channels, neural network intuition, deep learning perception, large language model analogy

Questions this chunk answers:
- How does a computer 'see' an image compared to a human?
- What is the underlying data structure of an image for a computer?
- What are the three color channels in an image?
- How do deep learning models process visual information?

chunk_text:
There are traditional computer vision techniques that people have worked on, such as manipulating color spaces, filtering, and edge detection. Edge detection is still very relevant. There are mathematical properties you can apply to smooth an image, convert it, and detect edges. These are classical computer vision techniques.

There are different color spaces. You can convert a 3-channel image into various color spaces. This is how traditional computer vision makes inferences. Libraries like OpenCV provide all the necessary transformations, so you don't have to write the code from scratch. You'll see in the notebook how we map original data into different color spaces.

Keywords: traditional computer vision, image processing techniques, color space conversions, filtering, edge detection, opencv, image manipulation

Questions this chunk answers:
- What are the basic techniques in traditional image processing?
- Why are color space conversions used in computer vision?
- What is OpenCV used for in image processing?
- How do traditional methods preprocess images?
